title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards for services and platform components: API design, coding conventions, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance targets, and the process for creating and recording ADRs. This document is intended for service owners, platform engineers, and reviewers onboarding new systems or auditing existing services.

Sections
1) API Standards
2) Coding Standards
3) Infrastructure Standards
4) Model-Serving Standards
5) Observability Standards
6) Performance Standards (SLOs & thresholds)
7) ADR process and recent decisions

1) API Standards
Intro: All public-facing and internal service APIs must be predictable, versioned, and discoverable. Design principles prioritize backward compatibility, explicit failure modes, and observable behavior.

Key rules:
- Use REST or gRPC consistently per service domain. Edge-facing endpoints should prefer REST/JSON; high-throughput internal RPCs should prefer gRPC.
- API versioning: include a major version in the path (e.g., /v1/, /v2/). No breaking change may be deployed to a major version without an ADR and a 30-day deprecation plan.
- Schema-first design: define request/response schemas (OpenAPI 3.0 for REST, proto3 for gRPC) and commit to the service repo under /api/*. API changes require CI validation against the canonical schema.
- Error model: use structured errors with fields: code (enum), message (short), details (optional). HTTP mapping: 400 (client), 401/403 (auth), 404 (not found), 409 (conflict), 429 (rate limit), 5xx (server).
- Idempotency: write APIs (POST/PUT) that can be retried must accept an idempotency key header (X-Idempotency-Key).
- Pagination: use cursor-based pagination for list endpoints (cursor, limit). Avoid offset pagination for production endpoints with high cardinality.
- Rate limiting: client tiering must be enforced at the gateway (see infra standards). Document per-route limits in API OpenAPI docs.

API Example (OpenAPI snippet):
```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Streaming text generation request
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Stream of tokens
```

Ownership and reviews:
- Every public API must list an API owner in the service README and register the API in the internal service catalog.
- API changes require a small design review: attach OpenAPI diff in PR and request sign-off from at least one API reviewer from eng-developer-experience.

2) Coding Standards
Intro: Consistent code quality accelerates onboarding and reduces incidents. These rules are minimums; team styleguides can add stricter constraints.

Key rules:
- Language choices: prefer Go for control plane and high-concurrency services; Python for evaluation/ETL tooling; Rust/C++ allowed for hot runtime paths only with architecture approval.
- Linting & formatting: use standard linters and formatters (gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff for Python). CI must fail on linter/formatter errors.
- Testing: unit tests >= 80% coverage on public package surface. Critical services (inference gateway, runtime-gateway, policy-router) require integration tests exercising failover and degraded capacity paths.
- Secrets: never commit secrets. Use HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS integrations. PRs that add secret scanning exceptions require security review.
- Dependency management: pin transitive dependencies, run weekly vulnerability scans, and upgrade within 30 days for high-severity CVEs.
- Documentation: every package/service must provide a README with: purpose, owner, deploy docs, and runbook link.

Code snippet: idempotent retry helper (Go):
```go
func DoWithIdempotency(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, req *http.Request, key string) (*http.Response, error) {
  req.Header.Set("X-Idempotency-Key", key)
  return client.Do(req.WithContext(ctx))
}
```

3) Infrastructure Standards
Intro: Infra standards ensure repeatable, observable deployments and predictable capacity. All infra changes must be expressed as code and reviewed.

Key rules:
- IaC: Terraform is the canonical tool for cloud resources. State must be remotely stored and access-controlled. Module registry must be used for common networking, IAM, and compute patterns.
- Network and security: services must follow least-privilege networking — private subnets for compute, NAT for egress, and security groups with explicit ports. Public endpoints require WG approval.
- Deployment: use our standard CI/CD pipelines (eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build) with canary by default (5% -> 25% -> 100%) and automated rollback on error budget or severe alerts.
- Capacity: GPU fleet autoscaling policies should be documented in gpu-fleet-and-capacity. Use predictive scaling for nightly batching workloads and reactive scaling for web-facing workloads.
- Secrets & keys: use KMS/HSM for key storage. Rotate keys annually or immediately on suspicion of compromise.

Example Terraform snippet (module usage):
```hcl
module "service_asg" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/modules/asg.git"
  name = "runtime-gateway"
  instance_type = "c7g.4xlarge"
}
```

4) Model-Serving Standards
Intro: Model-serving is the core differentiator. Standards focus on reproducible model variants, kernel/quantization metadata, traffic routing, and safe rollouts.

Key rules:
- Model packaging: all models must be stored in the model registry with immutable version IDs and metadata: architecture, weights checksum, tokenizer checksum, quantization profile, supported max_seq_len, and expected throughput (tokens/sec).
- Execution profiles: record kernel selection hints, recommended batch sizes, KV cache behavior, and memory footprint as part of the model metadata.
- Rollouts: use staged rollouts with QA shadow traffic, canary (1% -> 10% -> 100%) and continuous quality monitoring. Canary must run for at least 24 hours and meet latency and quality gates.
- Fallbacks: define a fallback model family in the routing policy (e.g., lower-precision quantized variant) with explicit quality degradation expectations.
- Latency-optimal paths: for single token low-latency requests, prefer pinned instances with small batch windows; for throughput jobs, use autoscaled batching pools.

Model manifest example (JSON-ish):
```json
{
  "model_id": "redwood-7b-v1.2.0",
  "checksum": "sha256:...",
  "quantization": "int8-ops",
  "max_seq_len": "4096",
  "recommended_batch": "8"
}
```

5) Observability Standards
Intro: Observability must make system behavior, performance regressions, and debugging fast and reliable. Instrumentation is required before launch.

Key rules:
- Metrics: emit domain metrics (requests_total, requests_failed, tokens_generated_total), service-level latency histograms (P50/P90/P95/P99), and resource metrics (GPU_utilization, mem_used_bytes). Use Prometheus exposition format.
- Tracing: include distributed tracing headers (traceparent/W3C). All request paths must be traceable across gateways, routers, runtime, and model execution.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with common fields: timestamp, service, env, trace_id, span_id, level, event, error (if any). Sensitive fields must be redacted prior to write or send via a secured pipeline.
- Dashboards: every service must publish a perf dashboard (latency, error rate, throughput, tokens/sec) and an alerts dashboard linked in the service README.
- Alerts: default SLO-aligned alerts (see Performance Standards). Alerts must include runbook links and suggested mitigations.

6) Performance Standards (SLOs & thresholds)
Intro: Performance standards are set by surface area: hosted API endpoints, dedicated capacity, and private deployments. SLOs are the contract between platform and customers.

Canonical SLO tiers (example values):
- Hosted API (standard tier): Latency SLO: 95th percentile < 300ms for single-token streaming requests; Availability SLO: 99.5% monthly; Error budget: 0.5%
- Dedicated (reserved): Latency SLO: 95th percentile < 250ms; Availability SLO: 99.9% monthly; Error budget: 0.1%
- Private (enterprise): negotiated SLAs. Default baseline: 95th percentile < 500ms; Availability SLO: 99.9%

Operational thresholds and alert mappings:
- Latency P95 breach > 15 minutes -> P1 page (oncall).
- Error rate increase > 3x baseline and > 0.5% absolute -> P1 page.
- GPU OOM rate > 0.1% of jobs -> P2 escalation to infra.

Testing and benchmarking:
- Every model onboarding must include a perf benchmark (latency distribution, tokens/sec, memory) in benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Benchmarks must be reproducible with pinned infra config.
- Run load tests for major releases and significant infra changes. Document test harness and test datasets used.

7) ADR process and recent decisions
ADR Process:
1. Create ADR draft in docs/adr/YYYYMMDD-short-title.md in the service repo.
2. Link the ADR in the central ADR index (this Confluence page's related_pages or the ADR index).
3. Request at least two approvers: one architecture representative and one affected service owner.
4. ADRs that change public API or infra defaults require a 7-day comment window and final sign-off from eng-platform.
5. After approval, add an entry to the service README and note the change in the monthly architecture digest.

Recent ADRs (summary):
- ADR-2026-03-01: Default RPC protocol for internal high-throughput services -> gRPC. Rationale: lower CPU serialization overhead and better streaming semantics. Owner: Daniel Kim.
- ADR-2026-02-15: Model quantization profiles allowed in hosted offering -> Accept int8-ops and int4-experimental with explicit quality guardrails. Owner: Priya Patel.
- ADR-2026-01-20: Standard canary rollout percentages and required QA duration -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with a minimum 24-hour canary. Owner: Service Reliability WG.

Template for ADR (to be used in repo):
- Title: short descriptive
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated
- Context: technical background and constraints
- Decision: the chosen option and why
- Consequences: operational and future implications
- Rollout plan: migration steps and timeline

Operational runbooks and links
- Each standard above references required runbooks (deploy, rollback, incident) in eng-platform/runbooks and eng-sre/runbooks. Ensure links are maintained in service READMEs.

Governance and enforcement
- Standards are reviewed quarterly by the Architecture Council. Exceptions require a documented risk & mitigation plan and sign-off by the council.
- Compliance checks: automated CI checks validate API schema, linting, test coverage, and presence of runbook links on PR. Infra PRs must pass terraform fmt and security scanning.

Appendix: Quick checklists
- New service checklist (must pass before production traffic):
  1) OpenAPI/proto committed and validated in CI
  2) README with owner and runbook
  3) Metrics, traces, and structured logs instrumented
  4) Automated tests (unit and integration) in CI
  5) Canary deployment pipeline configured
  6) Perf benchmark and expected capacity documented

- Model onboarding checklist:
  1) Model artifact uploaded to registry with metadata and checksum
  2) Perf benchmark completed and recorded
  3) Quantization profile and kernel hints documented
  4) Canary routing policy configured with fallback
  5) Quality evaluation tests (prompt set) added
